subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
classification: 69 original MEDSHUBH examiner-style PYQ/PYT-based practice questions; none claimed as verbatim recalled PYQs

questions.q: A 7-week pregnant patient has unilateral pelvic pain, spotting, shoulder-tip pain and hypotension. FAST shows free intraperitoneal fluid; no intrauterine pregnancy is seen. What is the next step?
o: Urgent resuscitation and operative management for ruptured ectopic pregnancy
questions.e: Haemodynamic instability, peritoneal/shoulder-tip pain and free fluid suggest ruptured ectopic pregnancy. Resuscitate, obtain urgent senior/operative review and do not delay definitive management for serial testing.
questions.b: Unstable + pain + free fluid = ruptured ectopic; resuscitate and operate.
optionExplanations: Serial β-hCG is for stable pregnancy of unknown location.
Correct: suspected rupture with shock requires emergency management.
Methotrexate is for selected stable, unruptured cases with follow-up.
Waiting is unsafe in suspected rupture.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH high-yield PYQ/PYT-based practice question; not a verified verbatim recalled PYQ.

questions.q: A stable patient has a pregnancy of unknown location, low β-hCG and no adnexal mass. Which approach is most appropriate?
o: Serial quantitative β-hCG and repeat transvaginal ultrasound
Ignore symptoms if β-hCG is low
questions.e: A stable pregnancy of unknown location requires structured follow-up with serial β-hCG and repeat TVUS. A single hCG value or empty uterus alone does not diagnose ectopic pregnancy.
questions.b: Stable PUL → serial β-hCG + repeat TVUS; do not treat a number alone.
optionExplanations: Not every PUL is ectopic; empiric methotrexate can harm a viable IUP.
Correct: follow trends and ultrasound while giving ectopic precautions.
Hysterectomy has no role.
Low hCG does not exclude ectopic pregnancy.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH high-yield PYQ/PYT-based practice question; not a verified verbatim recalled PYQ.

questions.q: A woman with recurrent miscarriage has a septate uterus on 3D ultrasound. Which uterine anomaly is classically associated with the highest miscarriage risk?
questions.e: A septate uterus is associated with adverse reproductive outcomes, especially miscarriage. Hysteroscopic septum incision may be considered in selected patients after counselling; evidence and indications should be individualized.
questions.b: Septate uterus → recurrent miscarriage association.
optionExplanations: Arcuate uterus is usually a mild variant with lower reproductive impact.
Correct: septum may impair implantation/placentation and is linked to miscarriage.
Unicornuate uterus is associated with preterm birth/malpresentation but is not the classic highest miscarriage association.
This is not the standard anomaly classification.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH high-yield PYQ/PYT-based practice question; not a verified verbatim recalled PYQ.

questions.q: A 32-week pregnant patient has a generalized tonic-clonic seizure and BP 170/112 mmHg. What is the first-line drug to prevent recurrent eclamptic seizures?
questions.e: Magnesium sulfate is first-line for treatment and prevention of recurrent eclamptic seizures. Stabilize airway/breathing/circulation, control severe BP and plan delivery after maternal stabilization.
questions.b: Eclampsia → magnesium sulfate; stabilize mother, then deliver.
optionExplanations: Phenytoin is not preferred over magnesium sulfate.
Correct: magnesium sulfate is first-line anticonvulsant in eclampsia.
Benzodiazepines may be used for refractory seizures, not routine preferred prophylaxis.
Valproate is not the standard treatment.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH high-yield PYQ/PYT-based practice question; not a verified verbatim recalled PYQ.

questions.q: A woman at 29 weeks has pre-eclampsia with severe features. Which finding is a severe feature even in the absence of proteinuria?
questions.e: Thrombocytopenia below 100,000/µL is a maternal end-organ severe feature. Other severe features include severe-range BP, renal impairment, liver dysfunction/persistent RUQ pain, pulmonary oedema and neurological symptoms.
questions.b: Pre-eclampsia severe feature: platelets <100,000/µL.
optionExplanations: Oedema is common and is not diagnostic/severe criterion by itself.
Correct: platelets <100,000/µL indicates severe feature.
Proteinuria amount alone does not define severe features.
Nausea alone is nonspecific.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH high-yield PYQ/PYT-based practice question; not a verified verbatim recalled PYQ.

questions.q: A patient with severe pre-eclampsia is receiving magnesium sulfate. She develops absent deep tendon reflexes and respiratory rate 8/min. What is the antidote?
questions.e: Loss of reflexes and respiratory depression suggest magnesium toxicity. Stop magnesium, support ventilation and give IV calcium gluconate according to protocol. Monitor urine output and serum magnesium when indicated.
questions.b: Magnesium toxicity → absent reflexes/respiratory depression; calcium gluconate antidote.
optionExplanations: Vitamin K reverses warfarin effect.
Correct: calcium gluconate antagonizes magnesium toxicity.
Atropine treats selected bradyarrhythmias.
Naloxone reverses opioid toxicity.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH high-yield PYQ/PYT-based practice question; not a verified verbatim recalled PYQ.

questions.q: A woman in active labour has a persistent fetal bradycardia and thick meconium with a high, unengaged presenting part. What is the priority?
o: Urgent assessment and expedited birth if fetal compromise persists
questions.e: Persistent fetal bradycardia is an intrapartum emergency. Stop uterotonics if running, summon help, assess reversible causes and expedite birth when compromise persists. Mode depends on cervical dilatation, station and urgency.
questions.b: Persistent fetal bradycardia → urgent intrauterine resuscitation and expedited birth.
optionExplanations: Delay risks hypoxic injury.
Correct: urgent assessment and timely birth are required.
Oxytocin may worsen tachysystole and fetal compromise.
Fundal pressure is not recommended.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH high-yield PYQ/PYT-based practice question; not a verified verbatim recalled PYQ.

questions.q: A labouring woman has a transverse lie with a live singleton fetus at term. What is the usual mode of delivery?
questions.e: Persistent transverse lie at term is generally delivered by caesarean section. Vaginal delivery is not possible for a singleton transverse lie unless special circumstances such as a second twin after delivery of the first.
questions.b: Singleton transverse lie at term → caesarean section.
optionExplanations: Vaginal delivery is obstructed in persistent transverse lie.
Correct: caesarean is the usual route for singleton transverse lie.
Vacuum requires a suitable cephalic presenting part and engaged head.
Forceps cannot correct a transverse lie.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH high-yield PYQ/PYT-based practice question; not a verified verbatim recalled PYQ.

questions.q: A primigravida at term has a fully dilated cervix, vertex at +2 station, position known, ruptured membranes and reassuring fetal status. Which instrument-assisted birth prerequisites are met?
o: Full dilatation, ruptured membranes, engaged head, known position and no disproportion
Unengaged head and unknown position are acceptable
Instrument can be applied before excluding CPD
questions.e: Safe operative vaginal birth requires full dilatation, ruptured membranes, engaged head, known position, adequate pelvis/no suspected CPD, appropriate analgesia, consent and immediate capability for caesarean if needed.
questions.b: Instrumental delivery prerequisites: fully dilated + engaged + known position + no CPD.
optionExplanations: Full dilatation alone is insufficient.
Correct: these are core prerequisites, with consent/analgesia and backup.
Unknown position/unengaged head makes application unsafe.
CPD must be excluded.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH high-yield PYQ/PYT-based practice question; not a verified verbatim recalled PYQ.

questions.q: After vaginal delivery, a woman has heavy bleeding and a boggy enlarged uterus. What is the first-line action?
o: Bimanual uterine massage and uterotonic treatment while activating PPH response
questions.e: Uterine atony is the commonest cause of PPH. Call for help, uterine massage, uterotonics (usually oxytocin first-line), IV access/resuscitation, quantify blood loss and follow the PPH bundle.
questions.b: PPH + boggy uterus = atony; massage + oxytocin + resuscitation.
optionExplanations: Correct: immediate uterine massage and uterotonic therapy are core first actions.
Hysterectomy is reserved for uncontrolled life-threatening bleeding after other measures.
Do not wait for labs before treating haemorrhage.
Anticoagulation worsens bleeding.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH high-yield PYQ/PYT-based practice question; not a verified verbatim recalled PYQ.

questions.q: A woman has persistent PPH despite uterine massage and oxytocin. The uterus remains atonic. Which intervention is a common next pharmacological option if no contraindication?
questions.e: Additional uterotonics include ergometrine/methylergometrine (avoid in hypertension), carboprost (avoid in asthma) and misoprostol, according to local protocol. Concurrently assess the four Ts and escalate.
questions.b: Atonic PPH: additional uterotonics; ergometrine contraindicated in hypertension.
optionExplanations: Correct: methylergometrine is an option if hypertension is absent.
Ritodrine is a tocolytic, not a PPH uterotonic.
Magnesium relaxes uterus and can worsen atony.
Terbutaline is a tocolytic.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH high-yield PYQ/PYT-based practice question; not a verified verbatim recalled PYQ.

questions.q: A woman with painless third-trimester bleeding has a placenta covering the internal cervical os on transvaginal ultrasound. Which diagnosis?
questions.e: Placenta covering the internal os is placenta previa. Painless bleeding is classic, although presentations vary. Avoid digital vaginal examination until placenta previa is excluded.
questions.b: Painless bleeding + placenta over os = placenta previa.
optionExplanations: Abruption classically causes painful bleeding/tender uterus, though bleeding may be concealed.
Correct: placental tissue covers the internal os.
Vasa previa involves fetal vessels over/near os.
Uterine rupture typically presents with pain, fetal compromise and maternal instability.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH high-yield PYQ/PYT-based practice question; not a verified verbatim recalled PYQ.

questions.q: A woman with previous caesarean deliveries has placenta previa and ultrasound features of placenta accreta spectrum. Which is the safest planned approach in a specialist centre for suspected placenta percreta?
o: Planned caesarean hysterectomy with placenta left in situ
questions.e: For significant placenta accreta spectrum, especially percreta, planned delivery in a multidisciplinary centre is essential. A common standard approach is caesarean hysterectomy with placenta left in situ; avoid forced placental removal because of catastrophic haemorrhage risk.
questions.b: Placenta accreta spectrum → do not forcibly detach placenta; specialist planned delivery.
optionExplanations: Manual removal can cause massive haemorrhage.
Correct: planned caesarean hysterectomy with placenta in situ is common standard management for severe PAS.
Unplanned labour/delivery is unsafe.
Curettage is dangerous.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH high-yield PYQ/PYT-based practice question; not a verified verbatim recalled PYQ.

questions.q: A fetus has estimated weight below the 3rd centile with abnormal umbilical artery Doppler. Which term best describes this?
questions.e: Estimated fetal weight below the 3rd centile is strongly concerning for fetal growth restriction, especially with abnormal Doppler. Distinguish pathological FGR from a constitutionally small fetus using growth trajectory, Doppler and clinical context.
questions.b: EFW <3rd centile and abnormal Doppler → FGR.
optionExplanations: Small for gestational age is a size descriptor and may be constitutionally small; abnormal Doppler supports FGR.
Correct: placental insufficiency and abnormal Doppler indicate pathological growth restriction.
Macrosomia is excessive fetal size.
LGA is >90th centile.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH high-yield PYQ/PYT-based practice question; not a verified verbatim recalled PYQ.

questions.q: In a growth-restricted fetus, which Doppler abnormality is generally the most concerning marker of advanced placental insufficiency?
o: Absent or reversed end-diastolic flow in umbilical artery
questions.e: Absent or reversed end-diastolic flow in the umbilical artery reflects severe placental vascular resistance and is associated with increased perinatal risk. Management depends on gestational age, ductus venosus/cardiotocography and maternal status.
questions.b: FGR + absent/reversed UA end-diastolic flow = severe placental insufficiency.
optionExplanations: MCA PI often falls with brain-sparing, rather than rises.
Correct: absent/reversed end-diastolic flow is a major adverse Doppler finding.
Normal UA Doppler is reassuring relative to abnormal flow.
A low CPR, not increased CPR, may indicate redistribution.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH high-yield PYQ/PYT-based practice question; not a verified verbatim recalled PYQ.

questions.q: A fetus has severe oligohydramnios and bilateral renal agenesis. Which mechanism explains the low amniotic fluid?
questions.e: After the mid-trimester, fetal urine is a major source of amniotic fluid. Bilateral renal agenesis causes absent fetal urine and severe oligohydramnios/anhydramnios, with pulmonary hypoplasia risk.
questions.b: Bilateral renal agenesis → absent fetal urine → oligohydramnios.
optionExplanations: Correct: fetal urine is a major contributor to amniotic fluid later in pregnancy.
Increased swallowing may reduce fluid but is not the mechanism in renal agenesis.
Maternal urine output does not determine amniotic fluid.
Fetal lung fluid is not the principal mechanism.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH high-yield PYQ/PYT-based practice question; not a verified verbatim recalled PYQ.

questions.q: A monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy develops oligohydramnios in one sac and polyhydramnios in the other, with a stuck donor twin. Diagnosis?
questions.e: The donor twin becomes hypovolaemic with oligohydramnios and the recipient hypervolaemic with polyhydramnios. This classic sequence in monochorionic twins suggests TTTS; stage and manage in a fetal medicine centre.
questions.b: MCDA twins + donor oligo/stuck twin + recipient poly = TTTS.
optionExplanations: TAPS is characterised by anaemia/polycythaemia without the classic oligo-poly sequence.
Correct: this is the classic TTTS presentation.
sFGR can coexist but does not explain the oligo-poly sequence.
Vanishing twin is early loss of one embryo.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH high-yield PYQ/PYT-based practice question; not a verified verbatim recalled PYQ.

questions.q: Which sign on first-trimester ultrasound most strongly supports dichorionic diamniotic twins?
questions.e: The lambda or twin-peak sign at the placental insertion of the intertwin membrane supports dichorionicity. The T-sign supports monochorionic diamniotic twins.
questions.b: Lambda sign = DCDA; T-sign = MCDA.
optionExplanations: T-sign is associated with MCDA.
Correct: lambda/twin-peak sign indicates chorionic tissue between membranes.
A single placental mass can occur in fused dichorionic placentas.
No membrane suggests MCMA, not DCDA.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH high-yield PYQ/PYT-based practice question; not a verified verbatim recalled PYQ.

questions.q: A 19-year-old with primary amenorrhoea has normal breast development, absent uterus, normal female external genitalia and 46,XY karyotype. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Complete androgen insensitivity is due to androgen receptor dysfunction in a 46,XY individual. Testes produce AMH, causing absent uterus; aromatisation supports breast development. Pubic/axillary hair is often sparse.
questions.b: 46,XY + breasts + absent uterus + sparse hair = complete androgen insensitivity.
optionExplanations: Müllerian agenesis is usually 46,XX with normal ovaries and normal androgen-dependent hair.
Correct: AMH causes absent uterus; androgen resistance causes female phenotype.
Turner is 45,X and usually has streak gonads/poor secondary sexual development.
Imperforate hymen causes outflow obstruction with uterus present.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH high-yield PYQ/PYT-based practice question; not a verified verbatim recalled PYQ.

questions.q: A 16-year-old has primary amenorrhoea, short stature, webbed neck, shield chest and streak ovaries. Which karyotype is most likely?
questions.e: Turner syndrome is classically associated with 45,X, gonadal dysgenesis, short stature, webbed neck and primary amenorrhoea. Evaluate cardiac and renal anomalies and provide hormone replacement when appropriate.
questions.b: Short stature + webbed neck + streak ovaries = Turner (45,X).
optionExplanations: 46,XX is typical female karyotype.
Correct: monosomy X is classic Turner syndrome.
47,XXY is Klinefelter syndrome.
46,XY does not fit the classic Turner phenotype.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH high-yield PYQ/PYT-based practice question; not a verified verbatim recalled PYQ.

questions.q: A woman with PCOS has oligomenorrhoea and obesity. Which long-term endometrial risk is increased by chronic anovulation?
questions.e: Chronic anovulation causes prolonged unopposed oestrogen exposure without regular progesterone withdrawal, increasing endometrial hyperplasia and cancer risk. Endometrial protection with cyclic progestin or combined hormonal contraception is considered when appropriate.
questions.b: PCOS + chronic anovulation → unopposed oestrogen → endometrial hyperplasia risk.
optionExplanations: Correct: unopposed oestrogen stimulates endometrium.
Cervical cancer is primarily linked to persistent high-risk HPV.
Germ-cell tumours are not the classic PCOS-associated risk.
No specific link.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH high-yield PYQ/PYT-based practice question; not a verified verbatim recalled PYQ.

questions.q: A patient with galactorrhoea and amenorrhoea has markedly raised prolactin. Which hypothalamic hormone normally inhibits prolactin secretion?
questions.e: Dopamine from the hypothalamus tonically inhibits prolactin release from anterior pituitary lactotrophs. Exclude pregnancy, medications and hypothyroidism; evaluate for prolactinoma when indicated.
questions.b: Prolactin is under tonic dopamine inhibition.
optionExplanations: GnRH stimulates LH/FSH.
Correct: dopamine inhibits prolactin.
TRH can stimulate prolactin.
Oxytocin mediates milk ejection, not tonic prolactin inhibition.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH high-yield PYQ/PYT-based practice question; not a verified verbatim recalled PYQ.

questions.q: A 52-year-old woman presents with postmenopausal bleeding. What is the essential principle of evaluation?
o: Exclude endometrial malignancy with appropriate endometrial assessment
Start combined oral contraceptive without investigation
questions.e: Postmenopausal bleeding requires evaluation to exclude endometrial cancer. Transvaginal ultrasound endometrial thickness and/or endometrial sampling is selected according to risk, imaging and persistence/recurrence.
questions.b: Postmenopausal bleeding = rule out endometrial carcinoma.
optionExplanations: Even scant bleeding needs assessment.
Correct: endometrial assessment is essential.
Hormonal treatment without evaluation may delay diagnosis.
Antibiotics do not evaluate the major concern.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH high-yield PYQ/PYT-based practice question; not a verified verbatim recalled PYQ.

questions.q: A 28-year-old with heavy menstrual bleeding has normal pelvic ultrasound, no structural lesion and wishes to avoid pregnancy. Which treatment is highly effective for reducing menstrual blood loss?
questions.e: The LNG-IUS is highly effective for heavy menstrual bleeding in suitable patients and provides contraception. Check contraindications and evaluate anaemia and underlying causes.
questions.b: Heavy menstrual bleeding + contraception desired → LNG-IUS is highly effective.
optionExplanations: Correct: local progestin causes endometrial suppression and reduces blood loss.
Copper IUCD may increase menstrual bleeding.
Tamoxifen can cause endometrial pathology.
Clomiphene induces ovulation and is not HMB treatment.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH high-yield PYQ/PYT-based practice question; not a verified verbatim recalled PYQ.

questions.q: A 30-year-old has severe dysmenorrhoea, deep dyspareunia and infertility. Laparoscopy shows powder-burn lesions. Diagnosis?
questions.e: Endometriosis is ectopic endometrial-like tissue, commonly causing dysmenorrhoea, deep dyspareunia and infertility. Powder-burn lesions are a classic laparoscopic appearance, although lesions vary.
questions.b: Dysmenorrhoea + deep dyspareunia + infertility + powder-burn lesions = endometriosis.
optionExplanations: Adenomyosis causes boggy enlarged uterus and dysmenorrhoea.
Correct: classic symptoms and laparoscopic appearance.
Polyps commonly cause intermenstrual/heavy bleeding.
PID causes infection-related pelvic pain/cervical motion tenderness.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH high-yield PYQ/PYT-based practice question; not a verified verbatim recalled PYQ.

questions.q: A woman with adenomyosis classically has which examination finding?
o: Uniformly enlarged, boggy and tender uterus
questions.e: Adenomyosis is endometrial glands/stroma within myometrium and classically causes a uniformly enlarged, boggy, tender uterus with dysmenorrhoea and heavy menstrual bleeding.
questions.b: Adenomyosis → uniformly enlarged boggy tender uterus.
optionExplanations: Small hard irregular uterus suggests fibroids may be irregular.
Correct: classic adenomyosis finding.
Barrel-shaped cervix suggests cervical pathology.
Ovarian mass with ascites raises concern for ovarian malignancy.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH high-yield PYQ/PYT-based practice question; not a verified verbatim recalled PYQ.

questions.q: A 35-year-old with submucosal fibroid has infertility and heavy menstrual bleeding. Which procedure is most appropriate for a cavity-distorting submucosal fibroid in a fertility-desiring patient?
questions.e: Hysteroscopic myomectomy is commonly used for accessible submucosal fibroids that distort the cavity in patients desiring fertility. Choice depends on size, type and depth.
questions.b: Submucosal cavity-distorting fibroid + fertility desire → hysteroscopic myomectomy.
optionExplanations: Correct: hysteroscopic resection restores cavity contour.
Hysterectomy eliminates fertility.
Oophorectomy is not indicated.
Endometrial ablation is unsuitable when future fertility is desired.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH high-yield PYQ/PYT-based practice question; not a verified verbatim recalled PYQ.

questions.q: A 34-year-old has persistent high-risk HPV positivity with abnormal cytology. Which test directly visualizes the transformation zone and guides biopsy?
questions.e: Colposcopy magnifies the cervix and transformation zone after application of acetic acid/Lugol iodine; directed biopsy establishes histology when indicated. Management follows age- and risk-based screening guidelines.
questions.b: Persistent hrHPV + abnormal cytology → colposcopy/biopsy as indicated.
optionExplanations: Correct: colposcopy evaluates cervical epithelium and guides biopsy.
HSG evaluates uterine cavity/tubal patency.
Laparoscopy evaluates peritoneal/pelvic structures.
Cystoscopy evaluates bladder.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH high-yield PYQ/PYT-based practice question; not a verified verbatim recalled PYQ.

questions.q: A cervical biopsy shows invasive squamous cell carcinoma. Which infection is most strongly associated with cervical cancer?
o: HSV-2 as the established necessary cause
questions.e: Persistent infection with high-risk HPV is the central causal factor in most cervical cancers; HPV16 and 18 are major oncogenic types. HPV 6/11 are low-risk types associated with genital warts.
questions.b: Cervical carcinoma → persistent high-risk HPV, especially 16/18.
optionExplanations: HPV 6/11 are low-risk wart-associated types.
Correct: HPV 16/18 are major oncogenic types.
EBV is linked to several other malignancies.
HSV-2 is not the established necessary cause.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH high-yield PYQ/PYT-based practice question; not a verified verbatim recalled PYQ.

questions.q: A 22-year-old has a unilateral ovarian mass. Histology shows Schiller-Duval bodies and serum AFP is raised. Diagnosis?
questions.e: Yolk sac (endodermal sinus) tumour occurs in younger patients, may produce AFP and shows Schiller-Duval bodies. It is a malignant germ-cell tumour.
questions.b: Schiller-Duval bodies + AFP = yolk sac tumour.
optionExplanations: Dysgerminoma may raise LDH and has fried-egg cells.
Correct: classic morphology and AFP marker.
Granulosa tumour may produce inhibin/oestrogen and Call-Exner bodies.
Mature teratoma contains mature tissues from germ layers.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH high-yield PYQ/PYT-based practice question; not a verified verbatim recalled PYQ.

questions.q: A 58-year-old has an ovarian mass, ascites and pleural effusion. CA-125 is elevated. Which syndrome is classically described?
questions.e: Meigs syndrome is the triad of benign ovarian fibroma, ascites and pleural effusion, resolving after tumour removal. CA-125 may be elevated and can mimic ovarian malignancy.
questions.b: Ovarian fibroma + ascites + pleural effusion = Meigs syndrome.
optionExplanations: Correct: classic triad.
Pseudo-Meigs is similar with other pelvic/abdominal tumours, not ovarian fibroma.
Sheehan is postpartum pituitary necrosis.
Asherman is intrauterine adhesions.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH high-yield PYQ/PYT-based practice question; not a verified verbatim recalled PYQ.

questions.q: A breastfeeding woman at 3 weeks postpartum asks for combined oral contraceptive pills. What is the best advice?
o: Avoid combined hormonal contraception in the early postpartum period; discuss suitable progestin-only/nonhormonal options
No contraception is needed during breastfeeding
questions.e: Combined hormonal contraception is generally avoided in the early postpartum period because of increased VTE risk and potential effects on lactation; eligibility timing depends on breastfeeding and thrombotic risk. Progestin-only and nonhormonal options may be appropriate.
questions.b: Early postpartum + breastfeeding → avoid combined estrogen-containing method; choose eligible alternative.
optionExplanations: Estrogen-containing methods are not routinely started at 3 weeks postpartum.
Correct: discuss progestin-only or nonhormonal contraception per eligibility.
Breastfeeding does not guarantee contraception unless strict LAM criteria are met.
Emergency contraception is not a daily method.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH high-yield PYQ/PYT-based practice question; not a verified verbatim recalled PYQ.

questions.q: A woman presents 4 days after unprotected intercourse and wants the most effective emergency contraception. Which option is generally most effective within 5 days?
o: Combined oral contraceptive taken for 21 days
Depot medroxyprogesterone injection as emergency contraception
questions.e: A copper IUCD inserted within 5 days is the most effective emergency contraception and provides ongoing contraception. Ulipristal or levonorgestrel pills are alternatives when appropriate, with timing and drug interactions considered.
questions.b: Emergency contraception within 5 days → copper IUCD most effective.
optionExplanations: Correct: copper IUCD has the lowest failure rate and ongoing benefit.
Combined OCP is not the standard emergency regimen.
DMPA is not an emergency contraceptive.
A future condom does not prevent pregnancy from prior intercourse.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH high-yield PYQ/PYT-based practice question; not a verified verbatim recalled PYQ.

questions.q: A couple has infertility. Semen analysis is abnormal on the first sample. What is the next appropriate step before diagnosing persistent male-factor infertility?
o: Repeat semen analysis after an appropriate interval with proper collection conditions
Proceed directly to IVF in every case
questions.e: Semen parameters vary; repeat analysis is needed when the initial result is abnormal, using standardized abstinence/collection and laboratory handling. Further evaluation is guided by repeat results and history.
questions.b: Abnormal semen analysis → repeat standardized sample before definitive classification.
optionExplanations: Correct: biological and technical variability require confirmation.
IVF is not automatic; investigate cause and couple factors.
Low motility is asthenozoospermia, not azoospermia.
Male evaluation is essential.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH high-yield PYQ/PYT-based practice question; not a verified verbatim recalled PYQ.

questions.q: A woman with regular 28-day cycles is being evaluated for ovulation. Approximately when should mid-luteal serum progesterone be measured?
o: About 7 days before expected next menses
questions.e: Progesterone should be measured in the mid-luteal phase, approximately 7 days before the expected next period (day 21 only in a 28-day cycle). A fixed day-21 test is inappropriate for longer/shorter cycles.
questions.b: Mid-luteal progesterone = ~7 days before next menses, not always day 21.
optionExplanations: Day 3 evaluates baseline ovarian hormones in selected workups.
Day 7 is usually follicular phase.
Correct: time it relative to expected menstruation.
Day 1 is early follicular phase.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH high-yield PYQ/PYT-based practice question; not a verified verbatim recalled PYQ.

questions.q: A 51-year-old has vasomotor symptoms and an intact uterus. If systemic estrogen therapy is prescribed, what must generally be added for endometrial protection?
questions.e: A woman with an intact uterus receiving systemic estrogen generally needs a progestogen to reduce endometrial hyperplasia/cancer risk. Estrogen-only systemic therapy is generally reserved for women without a uterus, subject to individual assessment.
questions.b: Intact uterus + systemic estrogen → add progestogen.
optionExplanations: Correct: progestogen protects endometrium from unopposed estrogen.
Testosterone is not endometrial protection.
Aromatase inhibitors are not used for this purpose.
Tamoxifen can increase endometrial pathology risk.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH high-yield PYQ/PYT-based practice question; not a verified verbatim recalled PYQ.

questions.q: A woman leaks urine when coughing and sneezing. Urinalysis is normal and postvoid residual is low. Most likely type?
questions.e: Leakage with raised intra-abdominal pressure (cough, sneeze, exercise) indicates stress urinary incontinence, commonly due to urethral hypermobility or sphincter deficiency.
questions.b: Cough/sneeze-associated leakage = stress incontinence.
optionExplanations: Correct: pressure-related leakage.
Urge is preceded by urgency.
Overflow is associated with retention/high residual.
Fistula causes continuous leakage.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH high-yield PYQ/PYT-based practice question; not a verified verbatim recalled PYQ.

questions.q: A woman has continuous leakage of urine per vagina after prolonged obstructed labour. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.e: Continuous urinary leakage after prolonged obstructed labour suggests vesicovaginal fistula due to pressure necrosis. Confirm with dye test/cystoscopy and assess ureteric involvement.
questions.b: Obstructed labour + continuous vaginal urine leak = VVF.
optionExplanations: Correct: classic obstetric fistula presentation.
Stress leakage is intermittent with effort.
Overactive bladder causes urgency/frequency, not continuous leakage.
Ureteric stone causes colic/haematuria.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH high-yield PYQ/PYT-based practice question; not a verified verbatim recalled PYQ.

questions.q: A woman has thin homogeneous vaginal discharge, fishy odour and clue cells on saline microscopy. Diagnosis?
questions.e: Bacterial vaginosis is a vaginal dysbiosis with thin homogeneous discharge, fishy odour, raised pH and clue cells. Treat symptomatic patients and selected special populations according to guidance.
questions.b: Clue cells + fishy odour + pH >4.5 = bacterial vaginosis.
optionExplanations: Candida causes itch, thick curdy discharge and normal pH usually.
Correct: clue cells are the classic microscopy clue.
Trichomonas shows motile organisms and often frothy discharge.
Gonorrhoea causes cervicitis/purulent discharge, not clue cells.

questions.q: A pregnant woman has confirmed syphilis. Which treatment is the only proven therapy to treat fetal infection and prevent congenital syphilis?
questions.e: Penicillin G is the only proven effective treatment for fetal infection and prevention of congenital syphilis. Pregnant patients with penicillin allergy should undergo desensitization and receive penicillin.
questions.b: Syphilis in pregnancy → penicillin G; desensitize if allergic.
optionExplanations: Doxycycline is contraindicated in pregnancy and does not reliably treat fetal infection.
Correct: penicillin is essential for fetal treatment/prevention.
Azithromycin resistance and inadequate fetal efficacy make it unsuitable.
Cefixime is not treatment for syphilis.

questions.q: A lactating woman has fever, breast erythema and wedge-shaped tenderness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Lactational mastitis presents with localized pain, erythema and systemic symptoms. Continue effective milk removal/breastfeeding when possible, provide analgesia and antibiotics when bacterial infection is suspected; assess for abscess if not improving.
questions.b: Lactation + fever + wedge erythema/tenderness = mastitis.
optionExplanations: Correct: typical presentation.
Fibroadenoma is a discrete benign lump without fever.
Duct ectasia causes nipple discharge/retraction, usually not acute febrile illness.
Cancer is considered for persistent atypical findings but is not the most likely acute presentation.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH high-yield PYQ/PYT-based practice question; not a verified verbatim recalled PYQ.

questions.q: A pregnant woman develops sudden dyspnoea, hypotension, hypoxia and DIC during labour. Which rare obstetric emergency is classically associated?
questions.e: Amniotic fluid embolism is a rare clinical syndrome with sudden cardiorespiratory collapse and coagulopathy/DIC during labour or shortly after delivery. Management is immediate supportive resuscitation and multidisciplinary critical care; no diagnostic test is definitive.
questions.b: Labour + sudden hypoxia/shock + DIC = amniotic fluid embolism.
optionExplanations: Correct: classic triad-like presentation.
Hyperemesis occurs early pregnancy and does not cause sudden DIC.
Molar pregnancy has abnormal trophoblastic proliferation.
Shoulder dystocia is mechanical delivery emergency.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH high-yield PYQ/PYT-based practice question; not a verified verbatim recalled PYQ.

questions.q: A woman with previous caesarean develops sudden abdominal pain, fetal bradycardia, loss of fetal station and maternal shock during labour. Diagnosis?
questions.e: Uterine rupture is a life-threatening complication, especially with a uterine scar. Sudden pain, fetal heart rate abnormality, loss of station and maternal haemorrhage/shock require immediate laparotomy and delivery.
questions.b: Previous CS + sudden pain + fetal bradycardia + loss of station = uterine rupture.
optionExplanations: Correct: classic warning signs.
Previa causes painless bleeding and does not cause loss of station in this pattern.
Cord prolapse causes fetal bradycardia but not maternal shock/abdominal signs.
Eclampsia is seizure in hypertensive disorder.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH high-yield PYQ/PYT-based practice question; not a verified verbatim recalled PYQ.

questions.q: After delivery of the fetal head, it retracts against the perineum and shoulders fail to deliver. What is the first-line manoeuvre?
questions.e: Shoulder dystocia is an obstetric emergency. Call for help, use McRoberts positioning and suprapubic pressure; avoid fundal pressure. Escalate to internal manoeuvres or other rescue techniques if needed.
questions.b: Turtle sign → shoulder dystocia; McRoberts + suprapubic pressure first.
optionExplanations: Correct: first-line manoeuvre combination.
Fundal pressure worsens impaction and is contraindicated.
Zavanelli is a rare last-resort manoeuvre.
Symphysiotomy is not routine first-line.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH high-yield PYQ/PYT-based practice question; not a verified verbatim recalled PYQ.

questions.q: An unsensitized RhD-negative pregnant woman has a potentially sensitizing event at 28 weeks. What prevents alloimmunization?
questions.e: Anti-D immunoglobulin prevents maternal sensitization to RhD-positive fetal red cells. Give according to gestational age, event and local protocol; assess fetomaternal haemorrhage when indicated.
questions.b: Unsensitized RhD-negative + sensitizing event → anti-D prophylaxis.
optionExplanations: Correct: passive anti-D prevents active maternal antibody formation.
MMR is a live vaccine and unrelated.
Magnesium treats/prevents eclamptic seizures.
Oxytocin stimulates uterine contraction.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH high-yield PYQ/PYT-based practice question; not a verified verbatim recalled PYQ.

questions.q: A RhD-negative mother is already sensitized with significant anti-D antibodies. What is the role of routine anti-D prophylaxis?
o: It is not effective once sensitization has occurred; monitor fetus for anaemia
Give double dose to remove antibodies
questions.e: Anti-D is prophylaxis, not treatment of established maternal alloimmunization. Once sensitized, assess antibody levels and fetal anaemia risk (e.g., MCA peak systolic velocity) and manage in specialist care.
questions.b: Anti-D prevents sensitization; it does not reverse established alloimmunization.
optionExplanations: It cannot remove established maternal immune memory/antibodies.
Correct: monitor fetal anaemia and plan specialist management.
Double dosing does not reverse sensitization.
Fetal anaemia may require intrauterine transfusion, not maternal anti-D.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH high-yield PYQ/PYT-based practice question; not a verified verbatim recalled PYQ.

questions.q: A 17-year-old has severe cyclic pelvic pain, primary amenorrhoea and a bluish bulging hymenal membrane. Diagnosis?
questions.e: Imperforate hymen causes outflow obstruction with primary amenorrhoea, cyclic pain and haematocolpos; a bulging bluish hymen may be seen. Confirm anatomy and treat with hymenotomy in appropriate setting.
questions.b: Primary amenorrhoea + cyclic pain + bulging bluish hymen = imperforate hymen.
optionExplanations: Correct: obstructed menstrual outflow leads to haematocolpos.
Endometriosis does not cause this obstructive hymenal finding.
PCOS causes oligo/anovulation, not cyclic obstructive pain.
Cervical cancer is not plausible in this presentation.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH high-yield PYQ/PYT-based practice question; not a verified verbatim recalled PYQ.

questions.q: A woman develops amenorrhoea after postpartum curettage for retained products. Hysteroscopy shows intrauterine adhesions. Diagnosis?
questions.e: Asherman syndrome is intrauterine adhesions, often following uterine instrumentation/infection, causing hypomenorrhoea/amenorrhoea and infertility. Hysteroscopy is diagnostic and therapeutic.
questions.b: Post-curettage amenorrhoea + intrauterine adhesions = Asherman syndrome.
optionExplanations: Correct: intrauterine synechiae.
Sheehan is postpartum pituitary infarction with lactation failure and hypopituitarism.
Turner is gonadal dysgenesis.
Adenomyosis causes heavy painful menses.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH high-yield PYQ/PYT-based practice question; not a verified verbatim recalled PYQ.

questions.q: A fetus has a lemon-shaped skull, banana-shaped cerebellum and myelomeningocele. Which association is most likely?
questions.e: Open spina bifida/myelomeningocele is associated with Chiari II malformation and characteristic lemon and banana signs on prenatal ultrasound. Offer detailed fetal assessment and counselling.
questions.b: Lemon sign + banana sign + myelomeningocele = Chiari II.
optionExplanations: Correct: classic association with open neural tube defect.
Dandy-Walker involves posterior fossa/vermis abnormalities.
Holoprosencephaly is forebrain cleavage defect.
Acrania is absent calvarium.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH high-yield PYQ/PYT-based practice question; not a verified verbatim recalled PYQ.

questions.q: A fetus has an omphalocele containing bowel and liver, covered by a membrane, with umbilical cord insertion at the apex. Which statement is correct?
o: It is usually not associated with chromosomal anomalies
Omphalocele is associated with chromosomal and other structural anomalies
It is always left-sided and uncovered
questions.e: Omphalocele is a midline defect at the umbilical ring, covered by a sac and often contains liver. It has significant association with aneuploidy and other structural anomalies. Gastroschisis is typically paraumbilical and uncovered.
questions.b: Omphalocele = midline + membrane-covered + associated anomalies/aneuploidy.
optionExplanations: Incorrect: omphalocele has important chromosomal associations.
Correct: detailed anomaly/genetic evaluation is indicated.
Gastroschisis is usually uncovered and paraumbilical.
Omphalocele is midline and membrane-covered.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH high-yield PYQ/PYT-based practice question; not a verified verbatim recalled PYQ.

questions.q: A 62-year-old has postmenopausal bleeding and endometrial biopsy confirms endometrioid carcinoma. Which risk factor is classically associated?
o: Multiparity as the strongest risk factor
questions.e: Endometrioid endometrial carcinoma is associated with unopposed estrogen exposure: obesity, chronic anovulation/PCOS, estrogen-only therapy and nulliparity among risk factors.
questions.b: Endometrioid endometrial cancer → unopposed estrogen.
optionExplanations: Correct: prolonged estrogen without progestogen increases risk.
Multiparity is generally protective.
Early menopause reduces lifetime estrogen exposure.
Combined OCP use is generally protective.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH high-yield PYQ/PYT-based practice question; not a verified verbatim recalled PYQ.

questions.q: A young woman has a rapidly growing ovarian mass and markedly elevated LDH. Histology shows large cells with clear cytoplasm and lymphocytes. Diagnosis?
questions.e: Dysgerminoma is the most common malignant ovarian germ-cell tumour, often in young women. It shows large cells with clear cytoplasm and lymphocyte-rich septa; LDH may be elevated.
questions.b: Young patient + ovarian mass + raised LDH + clear cells = dysgerminoma.
optionExplanations: Correct: characteristic morphology and marker association.
Yolk sac tumour has Schiller-Duval bodies and AFP.
Mucinous cystadenoma is epithelial and usually benign.
Brenner tumour has transitional-type cells and coffee-bean nuclei.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH high-yield PYQ/PYT-based practice question; not a verified verbatim recalled PYQ.

questions.q: A woman at 40 weeks has rupture of membranes, fever, uterine tenderness and fetal tachycardia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Maternal fever with uterine tenderness and fetal tachycardia after membrane rupture suggests intra-amniotic infection. Start broad-spectrum antibiotics, antipyretics/supportive care and proceed with delivery; infection alone is not an indication for caesarean.
questions.b: ROM + maternal fever + uterine tenderness + fetal tachycardia = chorioamnionitis.
optionExplanations: Correct: clinical features support intra-amniotic infection.
Accreta is abnormal placental adherence.
Vasa previa causes fetal bleeding after membrane rupture.
Inversion occurs after delivery with haemorrhage/shock.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH high-yield PYQ/PYT-based practice question; not a verified verbatim recalled PYQ.

questions.q: A woman on day 5 postpartum has fever, lower abdominal pain and foul-smelling lochia. Most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Postpartum endometritis presents with fever, uterine tenderness/lower abdominal pain and foul lochia. Treat with broad-spectrum IV antibiotics according to local protocol and assess for retained products or sepsis.
questions.b: Postpartum fever + uterine tenderness + foul lochia = endometritis.
optionExplanations: Correct: classic postpartum uterine infection.
Mastitis causes breast pain/erythema.
DVT causes limb swelling/pain.
Thyroiditis does not cause foul lochia or uterine tenderness.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH high-yield PYQ/PYT-based practice question; not a verified verbatim recalled PYQ.

questions.q: A sexually active woman has lower abdominal pain, cervical motion tenderness and adnexal tenderness. What is the recommended principle?
o: Delay antibiotics until laparoscopy confirms PID
Treat presumptively for PID when clinical threshold is met
questions.e: PID is a clinical diagnosis. In a sexually active patient with pelvic/lower abdominal pain and cervical motion, uterine or adnexal tenderness without a better explanation, initiate empiric broad-spectrum treatment promptly. Test for STI and manage partners.
questions.b: Pelvic pain + cervical motion/uterine/adnexal tenderness → low threshold for empiric PID treatment.
optionExplanations: Delaying treatment increases risk of infertility and ectopic pregnancy.
Correct: treat promptly when minimum clinical criteria are met.
Both patient and partners require appropriate management.
PID is usually polymicrobial bacterial infection, not fungal.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH high-yield PYQ/PYT-based practice question; not a verified verbatim recalled PYQ.

questions.q: A woman with primary amenorrhoea has normal secondary sexual characteristics, uterus present and elevated FSH. Which category is most likely?
o: Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism due to gonadal failure
questions.e: Elevated FSH with low estrogen suggests primary ovarian insufficiency/gonadal dysgenesis (hypergonadotropic hypogonadism). Interpret with repeat testing, age, karyotype and clinical context.
questions.b: High FSH + low estrogen = hypergonadotropic hypogonadism / ovarian failure.
optionExplanations: Hypogonadotropic states have low/normal FSH.
Correct: high FSH reflects reduced ovarian negative feedback.
Outflow obstruction generally has normal ovarian hormones and secondary characteristics.
Pregnancy does not cause this pattern.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH high-yield PYQ/PYT-based practice question; not a verified verbatim recalled PYQ.

questions.q: Which medication is contraindicated for treatment of postpartum haemorrhage in a woman with severe asthma?
questions.e: Carboprost (15-methyl PGF2α) can cause bronchospasm and is avoided in asthma. Select uterotonics according to contraindications; oxytocin is usually first-line.
questions.b: Asthma + PPH → avoid carboprost.
optionExplanations: Correct: prostaglandin F2α analogue may cause bronchospasm.
Oxytocin is first-line uterotonic in most settings.
Misoprostol is a prostaglandin E1 analogue and is an option.
Tranexamic acid is an antifibrinolytic adjunct, not a uterotonic.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH high-yield PYQ/PYT-based practice question; not a verified verbatim recalled PYQ.

questions.q: A woman at 31 weeks is at risk of imminent preterm birth. Which intervention accelerates fetal lung maturation?
questions.e: Antenatal corticosteroids (betamethasone or dexamethasone) reduce neonatal respiratory distress and other complications when preterm birth is likely within the recommended gestational window. Follow current local guideline criteria.
questions.b: Threatened preterm birth in eligible gestation → antenatal corticosteroids.
optionExplanations: Correct: corticosteroids accelerate surfactant production and fetal maturation.
Methotrexate is an antimetabolite used in selected ectopic pregnancy/oncology.
Warfarin is an anticoagulant and teratogenic.
Ergometrine is a uterotonic used postpartum.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH high-yield PYQ/PYT-based practice question; not a verified verbatim recalled PYQ.

questions.q: A 34-week pregnant woman presents with painless, bright-red vaginal bleeding. She is haemodynamically stable and the fetus is alive. What is the safest next step before deciding the mode of delivery?
o: Digital vaginal examination to assess dilatation
Ultrasound to locate the placenta; avoid digital vaginal examination until placenta praevia is excluded
questions.e: Painless antepartum haemorrhage suggests placenta praevia. Ultrasound localization is required; digital vaginal examination can precipitate catastrophic bleeding and is avoided until praevia is excluded. Stabilize and assess mother and fetus.
questions.b: APH + painless bright-red bleed = placenta praevia until excluded; NO digital PV examination.
optionExplanations: Digital PV examination may provoke severe haemorrhage.
Correct: locate placenta by ultrasound and avoid digital PV exam until praevia excluded.
Induction is unsafe before placental location and maternal-fetal assessment.
Amniotomy is not a diagnostic step and may cause harm.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH examiner-style PYQ/PYT-based practice; not a verified verbatim/recalled PYQ.

questions.q: A 36-week pregnant patient has sudden painful vaginal bleeding, a tense tender uterus and fetal bradycardia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Painful bleeding with uterine tenderness/hypertonicity and fetal compromise is classic for placental abruption. Bleeding may be concealed, so visible blood loss can underestimate severity.
questions.b: Painful APH + tender/woody uterus = abruption; concealed haemorrhage possible.
optionExplanations: Praevia classically causes painless bleeding.
Correct: abruption causes painful bleeding, uterine tenderness and fetal compromise.
Vasa praevia causes fetal blood loss after membrane rupture, often with fetal collapse.
Ectropion causes contact bleeding, not a tender hypertonic uterus.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH examiner-style PYQ/PYT-based practice; not a verified verbatim/recalled PYQ.

questions.q: Immediately after vaginal birth, a woman has brisk bleeding and a boggy uterus. After calling for help and uterine massage, which uterotonic is generally first-line?
questions.e: Uterine atony is the commonest cause of primary PPH. Initiate the PPH response, uterine massage, oxytocin and resuscitation concurrently; add further agents according to contraindications and protocol.
questions.b: 4 Ts: Tone is commonest; atonic PPH → massage + oxytocin first-line.
optionExplanations: Correct: oxytocin is first-line uterotonic for atonic PPH.
Carboprost is an additional option but avoid in asthma.
Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertension/pre-eclampsia.
Do not delay treatment for imaging.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH examiner-style PYQ/PYT-based practice; not a verified verbatim/recalled PYQ.

questions.q: A woman with PPH remains haemorrhagic despite uterine massage and oxytocin. She has severe bronchial asthma. Which uterotonic should be avoided?
o: None; carboprost is preferred in asthma
questions.e: Carboprost (15-methyl PGF2α) can cause bronchospasm and is avoided in asthma. Select an alternative uterotonic based on BP, contraindications and local PPH protocol; give tranexamic acid early when indicated.
questions.b: PPH + asthma → avoid carboprost; hypertension → avoid ergometrine.
optionExplanations: Correct: carboprost can precipitate bronchospasm.
Misoprostol may be used as an alternative uterotonic.
Oxytocin is generally first-line.
Carboprost is not preferred in asthma.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH examiner-style PYQ/PYT-based practice; not a verified verbatim/recalled PYQ.

questions.q: A woman develops PPH 20 minutes after birth. Which statement about tranexamic acid is most accurate?
o: Give as early as possible and within 3 hours of birth when PPH is diagnosed, alongside standard care
Use only if platelet count is low
questions.e: TXA is an antifibrinolytic adjunct for diagnosed PPH and should be administered as early as possible, within 3 hours of birth, in addition to standard care. It does not replace uterotonics, source control or resuscitation.
questions.b: TXA for PPH: early, within 3 hours; adjunct—not a uterotonic.
optionExplanations: Late administration beyond 3 hours is not recommended for PPH benefit.
Correct: administer early within 3 hours alongside standard PPH care.
TXA does not replace uterotonics or resuscitation.
It is not restricted to thrombocytopenia.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH examiner-style PYQ/PYT-based practice; not a verified verbatim/recalled PYQ.

questions.q: A 30-week pregnant woman reports a gush of fluid. Sterile speculum examination shows pooling; she is afebrile, not contracting and fetal status is reassuring. What is the best initial approach?
o: Assess gestation, infection and fetal status; manage PPROM expectantly when appropriate with latency antibiotics and antenatal corticosteroids per protocol
questions.e: PPROM at 30 weeks with no infection, labour or fetal compromise is generally managed expectantly in hospital/appropriate setting: confirm diagnosis, assess maternal-fetal status, give latency antibiotics and corticosteroids when eligible; magnesium for neuroprotection if imminent early preterm birth per guideline.
questions.b: PPROM stable + preterm → expectant care, antibiotics + steroids; avoid repeated digital PV exams.
optionExplanations: Repeated digital examinations increase infection risk.
Correct: expectant management with infection surveillance and gestation-appropriate interventions.
PPROM alone is not an automatic indication for caesarean.
Close monitoring, counselling and clear delivery triggers are essential.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH examiner-style PYQ/PYT-based practice; not a verified verbatim/recalled PYQ.

questions.q: A woman with PPROM at 31 weeks develops fever, uterine tenderness and fetal tachycardia. What is the priority?
o: Treat suspected intra-amniotic infection with broad-spectrum antibiotics and proceed to delivery
questions.e: Maternal fever, uterine tenderness and fetal tachycardia suggest intra-amniotic infection. Start broad-spectrum antibiotics, stabilize and proceed to delivery; infection alone does not mandate caesarean—route depends on obstetric indications.
questions.b: PPROM + chorioamnionitis → antibiotics + delivery; not prolonged expectant care.
optionExplanations: Expectant care is inappropriate with suspected infection.
Correct: antibiotics and delivery after stabilization.
Tocolysis is not appropriate in suspected intra-amniotic infection.
Repeated digital examinations increase ascending infection risk.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH examiner-style PYQ/PYT-based practice; not a verified verbatim/recalled PYQ.

questions.q: During vaginal birth, the fetal head delivers but retracts tightly against the perineum (“turtle sign”). What is the first manoeuvre?
o: Forceful traction on the fetal head
Immediate Zavanelli manoeuvre as first step
questions.e: Turtle sign indicates shoulder dystocia. Call for help, note time, perform McRoberts with suprapubic pressure; avoid fundal pressure and excessive traction. Proceed through an organized manoeuvre sequence if unresolved.
questions.b: Turtle sign → shoulder dystocia; McRoberts + suprapubic pressure; NEVER fundal pressure.
optionExplanations: Correct: first-line manoeuvre is McRoberts, often with suprapubic pressure.
Fundal pressure worsens impaction and risks injury.
Excessive traction risks brachial plexus injury.
Zavanelli is a last-resort manoeuvre, not first-line.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH examiner-style PYQ/PYT-based practice; not a verified verbatim/recalled PYQ.

questions.q: In shoulder dystocia, which action is specifically contraindicated?
questions.e: Fundal pressure can worsen shoulder impaction and increase maternal/fetal injury. Use McRoberts, suprapubic pressure and appropriate internal manoeuvres; document timings and manoeuvres.
questions.b: Shoulder dystocia: no fundal pressure; no excessive downward traction.
optionExplanations: Calling for help is essential.
McRoberts is a first-line manoeuvre.
Suprapubic pressure helps disimpact the anterior shoulder.
Correct: fundal pressure is contraindicated.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH examiner-style PYQ/PYT-based practice; not a verified verbatim/recalled PYQ.

questions.q: A fetus at 32 weeks has estimated fetal weight at the 4th centile, abdominal circumference at the 2nd centile and umbilical artery Doppler with absent end-diastolic flow. Which interpretation is best?
o: Constitutionally small fetus with reassuring Doppler
Fetal growth restriction with abnormal placental resistance requiring specialist surveillance and delivery planning
questions.e: EFW/AC below the 10th centile raises concern for FGR; absent end-diastolic flow in the umbilical artery is a high-risk Doppler finding reflecting increased placental resistance. Requires specialist surveillance and gestation-specific delivery planning.
questions.b: FGR + absent UA end-diastolic flow = high-risk placental insufficiency.
optionExplanations: Abnormal Doppler makes simple constitutional smallness less likely.
Correct: FGR with absent end-diastolic flow needs close specialist management.
Macrosomia is excessive fetal size.
This is not a normal Doppler finding.
questions.src: Original MEDSHUBH examiner-style PYQ/PYT-based practice; not a verified verbatim/recalled PYQ.

questions.q: In monochorionic diamniotic twins, one sac has oligohydramnios with a stuck twin and the other has polyhydramnios. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: The donor twin develops oligohydramnios and the recipient polyhydramnios in TTTS due to unbalanced placental vascular anastomoses in monochorionic twins. Assess by ultrasound and refer to fetal medicine; fetoscopic laser is standard treatment for eligible severe disease.
questions.b: Monochorionic twins + donor oligo / recipient poly = TTTS.
optionExplanations: TRAP has an acardiac twin perfused by the pump twin.
Correct: classic TTTS fluid discordance.
sFGR is discordant growth and Doppler abnormality, not the defining oligo-poly sequence.
Vanishing twin is early demise/resorption of one twin.
